newsitem.title: USA: U.S. recoups Gillette-Duracell insider gains.
newsitem.headline: U.S. recoups Gillette-Duracell insider gains.

text.p: Federal regulators said Monday they won judgments of about $2.8 million against traders who used inside information to profit on Duracell International Inc.'s merger with Gillette Co.

U.S. District Judge Shira Scheindlin in New York ordered a Swiss firm, Lennox, S.A., to return $450,699 in illegal profits and "certain unknown purchasers" trading through a Bahamian account to return $603,275 and pay a $1.77 million fine, the Securities and Exchange Commission said.

Lennox, which had discretionary authority over the account that traded in Duracell securities, consented to the court's judgment against it but did not admit or deny the allegations it engaged in insider trading, the SEC said.
The Bahamian account holders, however, did not appear for a court appearance, according to Paul Gerlach, an attorney in the SEC's Enforcement Division.
Gerlach declined to say whether the investigators knew the identity of the traders, who dealt through accounts at the Bahamian firm Nominees (Bahamas) Ltd.
"All I can say is that our investigation is continuing," said Gerlach.

The SEC said it was able to collect the $603,275 in illicit profits from the Bahamian account because the assets were frozen by a court order after the agency filed its civil complaint in the case Sept. 16. But the $1.77 million fine, nearly the maximum triple-damage amount the SEC is permitted to seek, remains uncollected, Gerlach said.
Even though the traders using the Bahamian account remain anonymous, the court's judgment against them will remain in effect if they are ever identified.
The court also issued orders against Lennox and the "unknown purchasers" that could subject them to more severe penalties if they violate federal securities laws in the future, the SEC said.

The SEC's Sept. 16 civil lawsuit, based largely on the circumstantial evidence of the timing and size of the dealings, accused unknown parties at the time of buying 1,700 call options -- rights to buy a stock at a given price -- for Duracell in the days before its merger with Gillette was announced Sept. 12.

The price of the options rose as the price of Duracell's stock jumped 27 percent at the time of the merger announcement, the complaint said. The options were later sold for a profit of about $950,000, it said.
